comments.text:
The Chagossians should be compensated (handsomely) for their displacement... but the idea of them 'reclaiming' any of the islands is preposterous (at least on an 'at scale' basis), given that the import/export infrastructure necessary to live there is prohibitively expensive. Unless you are a) independently wealthy, like millionaire status, or b) willing/able to live on a seafood/coconut/kelp subsistence lifestyle with almost no way to gain income... there's no way they could sustain themselves there. Even commercial fishing, as rich as those waters may be, would be insanely difficult. Whatever you catch, you have to transport thousands of miles to be able to sell. How would you even get fuel for your boats? 
 Their initial existence there emerged from an economic bubble sustained by massive corporations selling coconuts to the world using slave/indentured labor. That infrastructure is long gone, and never should have been there in the first place. There's a reason no one lived there before these colonialist powers took over. And yes, as recently as the early 1970s, there were people there making it work... but most of them are no longer with us, and with their passing, so went the local knowledge of how sustain themselves on such isolated islands. I have a hard time imagining that Chagossian descendants who have never set foot there, who have lived their entire life in the UK, would be able to re-capture the island subsistence way of life their grandparents and great-grandparents scraped together for themselves. Perhaps there are some descendants living on Mauritius or the Maldives who still know how to live that life... but any Chagossians who have been living in the UK for the last 5+ decades... no way. They could not function there any better than I could if I were plopped down onto one of my ancestors' East Tennessee dairy or tobacco farms from 60 years ago (I'm now a 21st century media worker in Chicago).

comments.text:
I'll start by saying that what the UK did was a crime. Refusing to return the land to its rightful inhabitants is also an injustice. HOWEVER, allowing people to return without addressing the long-term consequences of climate change could create another injustice. We could effectively be sentencing their descendants to an increasingly dangerous future as rising sea levels threaten their homes and livelihoods.

One possible alternative would be for the UK and US to pay substantial reparations to every descendant, including purchasing land on a larger, more geographically stable island where they could establish a permanent community. Ideally, this would be somewhere that could provide both security and the opportunity to preserve their cultural identity.

Most importantly, the Chagossians themselves must be directly involved in these discussions and have a meaningful say in determining their own future.

Obviously, this wouldn't undo the original injustice, but it might offer a more sustainable solution than simply returning people to islands increasingly threatened by climate change.

I am NOT advocating for any of the current or potential future resolutions for the future of the Chagossians. But I do have one logistical question. Can the Chagos islands realistically support a population of 10,000+ people? I'm talking both physically and economically. I suspect the 2000 military personnel are already living pretty much cheek-by-jowl on Diego Garcia. Ecotourism could be an immediately developable economic resource, but it's self-limiting - too much and you destroy the resources the ecotourists are coming to see. Perplexing problems, indeed.

comments.author: @takeshikovacs1531
comments.text:
This conversation is ridiculous. Chagosian people/culture is not a thing. Those people are from all over Indian ocean territory. They were brought to the archipelago by Europeans and spent 150 years there. They managed to build some shacks for shelter (probably with the assistance of Europeans) and come up with a few dances. One can barely call it a culture. When the British came back to the archipelago in the 50s, those people still had no government structure. They are glorified survivolists.

Empires throughout history had expansion campaigns. They gain and lose territories. Whoever or whatever nation had a claim for the Chago Archipelago before the British conquest, they lost it. It is very generous for Great Britain to give back some of those islands and territories. It is ludacrious to demand the archipelago that you lost hundreds of years ago.
